essentialQuestion.source: Why does AI sometimes work well for some people and badly for others?
essentialQuestion.back: Why does AI sometimes work well for some people and badly for other people?

learningGoal.source: Explain how who is in the data, and other causes, can make an AI tool work worse for some groups of people, and why a gap in results shows a problem but not its cause.
learningGoal.back: Explain how who is in the data, and other causes, can make an AI tool work worse for some groups of people, and why a gap in results shows there is a problem but does not show its cause.

read.sections.0.text.source: At Riverbend Learning Centre, a team tested a voice typing tool. Teachers, older learners and the youngest learners each read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers, with 19 words right. For the youngest learners, it got only 9 right. The gap shows that the tool works worse for young children. It does not show why. So the team looked for a cause. The tool had learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were new to it. Researchers have found this in real speech tools too. In a 2024 study, a widely used tool made several times as many mistakes with children's speech as with adults'. The researchers gave two reasons: there are far fewer recordings of children, and children's speech changes a lot as they grow.
read.sections.0.text.back: At Riverbend Learning Centre, a team tested a voice typing tool. The teachers, the older learners and the youngest learners each read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers, with 19 words right. For the youngest learners, the tool got only 9 words right. This gap shows that the tool works worse for young children. This gap does not show why. So the team looked for the cause. The tool learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were new to it. Researchers have also found this in real speech tools. In a 2024 study, a widely used tool made several times more mistakes on children's speech than on adults' speech. The researchers gave two reasons: there are far fewer recordings of children, and children's speech changes a lot as they grow.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Riverbend, a team tested a voice typing tool. Teachers and learners each read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers. It got 19 right. For the youngest learners, it got only 9 right. The gap shows a problem for young children. But it does not show the reason. So the team looked for one. The tool learned mostly from adult voices. Children's voices were new to it. In 2024, researchers found a real tool made many more mistakes with children. There are fewer recordings of children. And children's speech changes as they grow.

The tool learned mostly from adult voices. Children's voices were new to it. In 2024, researchers tested a real tool. It made many more mistakes for children. There are fewer recordings of children. And children's speech changes as they grow.

read.sections.1.text.source: When a tool works well for some groups of people and badly for others, we say it has a bias. One cause is the training data. Does it represent everyone who will use the tool? A famous collection of more than a million photos has been used to train many tools. About 45% of its photos were taken in the United States, and only about 2% in India. Researchers found that a tool trained on it was worse at naming things in photos from India or Pakistan, such as a bridegroom at a wedding. Nobody had to plan this for the result to be unfair.
read.sections.1.text.back: When a tool works well for some groups of people and badly for other groups, we say the tool has a bias. One of its causes is the training data. Does that data represent everyone who will use the tool? A famous collection of more than a million photos has been used to train many tools. About 45% of its photos were taken in the United States, and only about 2% in India. Researchers found that a tool trained on that photo collection was worse at recognising what is in photos from India or Pakistan, for example a bridegroom at a wedding. The result can be unfair even though nobody planned it.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Nobody had to plan this for the result to be unfair" as "the result can be unfair even though nobody planned it", in both readings; the teachers' note asks that bias is not called always accidental, and this wording keeps that open. "Naming things in photos" as "mengenali apa yang ada di foto" (recognising what is in photos), since a bridegroom is a person, not a thing.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some tools work well for some people and badly for others. This is called bias. One cause is the training data. Does the data represent all the people who will use the tool? One big set of photos has trained many tools. Almost half its photos came from the United States. Very few came from India. A tool trained on it did worse with photos from India or Pakistan. Nobody had to plan this for it to be unfair.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Some tools work well for some people and badly for others. This is called bias. One of its causes is the training data. A tool trained with it did worse with photos from India or Pakistan. The result can be unfair, even though nobody meant it to be.

read.sections.2.heading.source: The same gap can have different causes
read.sections.2.heading.back: The same gap can have different causes

read.sections.2.text.source: Two computer scientists described two made-up cases to explain this. In the first, a hospital tool missed more heart attacks in women than in men. The researcher added more records from women, and the tool improved. In the second, a hiring tool said women were less suitable for jobs. It had learned from people's past ratings of workers, and those ratings were unfair to women. Adding more of the same kind of data did not help. Both tools showed the same kind of gap, but the causes were different. Other causes include a tool's goal, its design, or using it in a place it wasn't made for. So people test a tool with many groups, look for the cause, and fix that.
read.sections.2.text.back: Two computer scientists described two made-up cases to explain this. In the first case, a hospital tool failed to recognise heart attacks more often in women than in men. The researcher added more records from women, and the tool got better. In the second case, a tool for choosing new workers said women were less suitable for jobs. The tool learned from people's ratings of workers in the past, and those ratings were unfair to women. Adding more data of the same kind did not help. Both tools showed the same kind of gap, but the causes were different. Other causes include a tool's goal, its design, or using it in a place it was not made for. So people test a tool with many groups, look for the cause, and fix that cause.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Hiring tool" as "alat untuk memilih pekerja baru" (a tool for choosing new workers), plainer than "alat rekrutmen" or "alat penerimaan karyawan"; the same words are used throughout the lesson.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Two scientists made up two cases to explain this. In the first, a hospital tool missed more heart attacks in women. They added more records from women, and it got better. In the second, a hiring tool said women were less suitable. It learned from people's past ratings, which were unfair to women. More of the same data did not help. Both tools had a gap, but the causes were different. A goal or design can cause it too. So people test a tool with many groups. Then they find the cause and fix it.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Two scientists made up two cases to explain this. In the first case, a hospital tool more often did not recognise heart attacks in women. watch.summary.source: This video explains why training data matters so much. A machine learning tool is only as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video site keeps track of what people watch, sometimes without them knowing. Then it uses that data to suggest more videos. In health care, experts label thousands of medical pictures, so a computer can learn to spot illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most of the X-ray pictures come from men. Then the tool may make more mistakes for women. People can put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data. Is there enough of it? Does it include many kinds of people and situations?
watch.summary.back: This video explains why training data is so important. A machine learning tool is only as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video site records what people watch, sometimes without them knowing. Then that site uses that data to suggest more videos. In health care, experts label thousands of medical pictures, so that a computer can learn to recognise illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most of the X-ray pictures come from men. Then the tool may make more mistakes for women. People can put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data. Is there enough data? Does that data include many kinds of people and situations?

educatorNotes.0.source: The Riverbend test and its numbers (19, 16 and 9 of 20) are made up; the evidence tells learners what the tool learned from, so the cause is given, not worked out from the scores. Real research: Kid-Whisper (Attia and others, AIES 2024) found that Whisper speech models, without extra training, had word error rates 6 to 10 times adults' on scripted children's speech and 3 to 5 times on conversational children's speech in the test sets it used. It names two causes: child speech databases are limited and hard to collect, and children's speech varies as they develop. Training on children's speech reduced errors, and the authors list remaining challenges. Photos: Suresh and Guttag (2021) report that about 45% of ImageNet's 1.2 million labelled images were taken in the United States, 1% in China and 2.1% in India, and cite a study (Shankar and others) finding that a classifier trained on it did significantly worse on images such as “bridegroom” from under-sampled countries like Pakistan or India.
educatorNotes.0.back: The Riverbend test and its numbers (19, 16 and 9 of 20) are made up; the evidence in the lesson tells learners what the tool learned from, so the cause is given, not worked out from the scores. Real research: Kid-Whisper (Attia and others, AIES 2024) found that Whisper speech models, without extra training, had word error rates 6 to 10 times adults' error rates on the speech of children reading a script, and 3 to 5 times on children's speech in conversation, in the test data sets it used. The study names two causes: databases of children's speech are limited and hard to collect, and children's speech keeps changing as they develop. Training with children's speech reduced errors, and the authors list the challenges that remain. Photos: Suresh and Guttag (2021) report that about 45% of ImageNet's 1.2 million labelled images were taken in the United States, 1% in China and 2.1% in India, and cite a study (Shankar and others) that found a classifier trained on it worked much worse on images such as “bridegroom” from countries under-represented in the sample, such as Pakistan or India.
educatorNotes.0.note: The image label "bridegroom" is kept in English (it is ImageNet's label), with "pengantin pria" in brackets.

educatorNotes.1.source: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag list seven sources of harm across the machine-learning life cycle: historical, representation, measurement (how labels are chosen), aggregation, learning (the goal a model is trained for), evaluation (how it is tested) and deployment (how and where it is used). Their heart-attack and hiring examples are a “simplified scenario” they made up to show that the same symptom can have different causes: more data from women helped the first, but not the second, where the labels came from biased human ratings. The lesson says so. A gap in results shows something is wrong, not why. Don't tell learners that bias is always an accident: the lesson says only that a result can be unfair even when nobody planned it. This lesson no longer repeats Lesson 3's model testing; the leaf model and the translation tool were taken out. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md.
educatorNotes.1.back: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag name seven sources of harm across the machine-learning life cycle: history, representation, measurement (how labels are chosen), aggregation, learning (the goal a model is trained for), evaluation (how a model is tested) and deployment (how and where a model is used). Their heart-attack and choosing-new-workers examples are a “simplified scenario” they made up to show that the same symptom can have different causes: more data from women helped the first case, but did not help the second, because its labels came from biased human ratings. The lesson says so. A gap in results shows that something is wrong, not why. Don't tell learners that bias always happens by accident: the lesson says only that a result can be unfair even when nobody planned it. This lesson no longer repeats the model testing from Lesson 3; the leaf model and the translation tool have been removed. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md.
educatorNotes.1.note: The seven sources' names are given in Indonesian with "agregasi" in brackets; the paper's own English names are historical, representation, measurement, aggregation, learning, evaluation and deployment.
